facts.text: The pied stilt is also known as the white-headed stilt.
facts.quote: The pied stilt (Himantopus leucocephalus), also known as the white-headed stilt, is a shorebird in the family Recurvirostridae.

facts.text: The pied stilt grows to about 36 cm long with a wingspan of about 67 cm.
facts.quote: The pied stilt grows to a length of about 14 in (36 cm) with a wingspan of about 26.5 in (67 cm).

facts.text: Its head, back and upper wings are glossy greenish-black, while the rest of its plumage is white.
facts.quote: The back of the head and neck, the back and the upper surfaces of the wings are glossy greenish-black. The undersides of the wings are plain black and the remainder of the plumage is white

facts.text: The pied stilt has long thin pink legs, and its irises and eyelids are red.
facts.quote: The long, thin legs are pink and the toes have black claws. The long slender beak is black and the irises and the eyelids are red.

facts.text: As it flies, the pied stilt gives a repeated yelping cry and its legs trail behind, swaying from side-to-side.
facts.quote: It emits a repeated yelping cry as it flies, and the legs trail behind it, tending to sway from side-to-side.

facts.text: In spring it nests in a shallow scrape, usually laying four yellowish-brown eggs dappled with dark blotches.
facts.quote: It prepares a nest in a shallow depression or in a scrape in the ground where it usually lays four, ovoido-conical eggs. These are yellowish-brown dappled irregularly with dark blotches and spots.

facts.text: Parent birds reveal their hidden nest by flying in circles and uttering distress cries.
facts.quote: The nest is difficult to find as the eggs are well-camouflaged. But the parent birds give away the presence of the nest by mounting into the air and flying in circles, uttering distress cries.

facts.text: A parent pied stilt sometimes feigns a leg injury to lure intruders away from its chicks, which freeze when alarmed.
facts.quote: The chicks are able to leave the nest almost as soon as they have hatched. They are difficult to detect because their downy plumage is well-camouflaged and they "freeze" when alarmed. A parent bird sometimes feigns a leg injury to draw intruders away from its chicks.
